issues.legal_issue: For land acquisitions initiated before the commencement of the amending legislation, entitlement to the additional compensation is confined to the transitional categories specified by the legislation.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications in these matters were issued in 1979, and the Land Acquisition Officer made the award in 1980, before the relevant transitional cutoff.
The reference court enhanced compensation in 1985, after the amending legislation came into force.
The High Court rejected the claim for the additional amount, and the claimants relied on the contrary decision in Union of India v. Zora Singh.
issues.conclusion: For acquisition proceedings initiated before the amending legislation commenced, the additional amount is payable only in the transitional categories corresponding to proceedings pending at the bill-introduction cutoff with no Collector’s award before that cutoff, or proceedings commenced after that cutoff. Zora Singh was overruled to the extent that it allowed the amount in every case pending before the reference court on commencement, irrespective of when the Collector made the award.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(1-A) creates a substantive right and is not retrospective absent clear legislative direction. It must be read together with Section 30(1), which specifies the extent to which that right applies to earlier acquisition proceedings; the transitional provision cannot be expanded by reading Section 23(1-A) in isolation. The Court endorsed Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama and the limited-retrospectivity approach in Union of India v. Raghubir Singh, and rejected the contrary construction in Union of India v. Zora Singh. The general presumption against applying new substantive law to pending matters is supported by United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum and Garikapatti Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhury.

issues.definition: A claimant in a pre-amendment acquisition proceeding qualifies for the additional compensation only if the proceeding falls within one of the two stated transitional categories.

issues.legal_issue: Limiting additional compensation to the legislatively specified transitional categories does not violate the constitutional guarantee concerning acquisition of certain agricultural land.
material_facts: It was argued that excluding acquisitions with Collector’s awards made before the transitional cutoff would leave compensation below the market value at the time possession was taken.
The challenge relied on the constitutional proviso concerning acquisition of land held under personal cultivation.
The legislation under which the land was acquired was pre-constitutional general land-acquisition legislation, not legislation relating to agrarian reform.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional guarantee concerning acquisition of agricultural land did not affect the interpretation of the additional-compensation provisions, and the transitional limitation did not violate that guarantee.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to Article 31-A(1) concerns laws providing for agrarian reform. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is not such a law; it is pre-constitutional legislation saved by Article 31(5)(a). Accordingly, Article 31-A does not govern the interpretation of Section 23(1-A) or Section 30(1) of the amending legislation. The Court relied on Atma Ram v. State of Punjab.

issues.definition: When land is acquired under a general pre-constitutional acquisition law, invoking the agricultural-land guarantee does not invalidate the transitional limit on additional compensation.

issues.legal_issue: The transitional cutoff for entitlement to additional compensation is not arbitrary merely because it distinguishes awards made on different sides of that cutoff.
material_facts: It was argued that two acquisitions arising from the same notification could receive different treatment if the Collector made one award before the cutoff and the other after it.

The Court held that the legislature could have confined the new benefit to awards made after the amending legislation commenced and that its decision to extend the benefit to a limited earlier period did not make the classification arbitrary.
The cutoff was the date on which the original amendment bill was introduced in Parliament.
issues.conclusion: The limited retrospective classification was not arbitrary or unconstitutional under Article 14; the cutoff did not require the benefit to be extended to awards made before it.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require the legislature to extend a newly created benefit to every earlier award merely because it has chosen to extend the benefit retrospectively to a defined period. The Court held that the selected cutoff was not arbitrary and that the limited retrospectivity in Section 30(1) did not render the provision unconstitutional.
